question: Why is model evaluation critical for addressing extreme risks from general-purpose AI, and how should dangerous-capability and alignment evaluations be built and embedded in governance?
hypothesis: Evaluations for dangerous capabilities and alignment, embedded in training, deployment, transparency and security processes, are a necessary (not sufficient) component of governance for extreme risks.
contributions: Argues for two evaluation classes: dangerous capability evaluations and alignment evaluations
Blueprint embedding evaluation in responsible training, deployment, transparency and security (Fig 4)
Table 1 list of dangerous capabilities and Table 2 desirable qualities of extreme risk evaluations
Limitations (six listed) and hazards (four) of such evaluations
Recommendations for frontier developers and policymakers

results.claim: In a 2022 survey of AI researchers, 36% thought AI could plausibly cause a catastrophe this century at least as bad as an all-out nuclear war.
results.setup: 2022 NLP community metasurvey of AI researchers cited as motivation
results.quote: In a 2022 survey of AI researchers, 36% of respondents thought that AI systems could plausibly “cause a catastrophe this century that is at least as bad as an all-out nuclear war”

results.claim: The paper defines extreme risk operationally as damage in the tens of thousands of lives or hundreds of billions of dollars, or severe disruption of social and political order.
results.quote: damage in the tens of thousands of lives lost, hundreds of billions of dollars of economic or environmental damage

results.claim: Evaluation results at the end of a long development process, especially after safety fine-tuning, will likely fail to convey information about the base model, so evaluate throughout the lifecycle.
results.quote: the results from the end of a long development process will likely fail to convey relevant information about the base model, especially if it has been fine-tuned for safety

results.claim: Capability overhang: chain-of-thought prompting raised GPT-3 performance months after release, so evaluations can miss latent capabilities.
results.quote: after GPT-3 had already existed for many months, researchers
results.note: Sentence continues on next page: demonstrated that chain-of-thought prompting could significantly increase performance

results.claim: Training on widely available safety evaluations can make models only superficially safe; keep private held-out evaluations.
results.quote: Developers and model auditors could therefore consider keeping some private “held out” evaluations

limits: No experiments or data; Figure 2 is purely illustrative.
Authors concede evaluation cannot catch all risks: factors beyond the AI system, unknown threat models, capability overhang, deceptive alignment, emergence, immature ecosystem, overtrust.
Evaluation is necessary but not sufficient; comprehensive alignment evaluation is expected to be hardest and is not solved.
Hazards: proliferating dangerous capabilities, competitive pressure, superficial safety, harms during evaluation.
Dated: written May 2023; named evaluations (ARC Evals, GPT-4 system card) are early efforts.
practices: Run internal evaluation, external research access and external audit (Sec 3).
Evaluate models during training at regular intervals and forecast from weaker models, including inverse-scaling analysis (Sec 3.1).
Delay or pause training on sufficiently concerning results (Sec 3.1).
Deploy gradually and continue evaluation and monitoring after deployment; review continuously (Sec 3.2, Fig 5).
Report incidents, share predeployment risk assessments, scientific reporting, educational demos (Sec 3.3).
Evaluate with and without system-level augmentations; surface latent capabilities via prompting or fine-tuning (Table 2).
Do not rely solely on behavioural evaluations; add mechanistic analysis (Sec 4, Table 2).
Keep private held-out evaluations to avoid training on the test (Sec 5.2).
Use honeypots, AI-written evaluations and breadth/targeting for alignment coverage (Sec 4).
